title: Krishna Rebukes Gandhari
story:
Gandhari had just cursed him, and Krishna had accepted the curse with a smile. Now he stood before her on the field of Kurukshetra, with the grief of a hundred dead sons hanging between them like weather.

Gandhari, mother of the hundred Kaurava brothers, had raised her hands over the battlefield and called down her curse on the man she held responsible for the slaughter: that he would die as her sons had died, at the hands of his own kinsmen. Krishna had taken the words as one takes a blessing. And now, before the pyres of the dead were even built, he spoke.

"Arise, arise, Gandhari," he said. "Do not set your heart on grief. Through your own fault this vast carnage has taken place. Your son Duryodhana was wicked at heart, envious, and swollen with pride. You applauded his wicked deeds and counted them good. He was cruel — hostility itself — and deaf to the counsel of his elders. And you: why do you wish to heap your own faults upon me?"

He did not say that the war had been fate, or that the gods had willed it. The fault, he told her, was hers. Then he spoke of grief itself. "Whoever grieves for what is already past," he said, "only gathers more grief — indulge it, and it doubles." Mourning, he told the mother of the dead, is a fire that feeds on itself.

Then came the harshest words of all. He spoke of the children different mothers bear: the priest's wife bears a son for prayer and penance, the cow her calf for burdens, the mare hers for speed, the serving woman hers for service, the cowherd's wife hers for the herds. "But a princess," Krishna said, "bears sons to be slaughtered."

Gandhari said nothing. The old accounts say her heart was torn by grief, and that she stood silent. Whatever she had expected from Krishna — comfort, apology, the name of the guilty — she received the truth instead, and the truth left her no reply.

Her husband, Dhritarashtra — the blind king of the Kurus — had been listening at her side, and it was he who broke the silence at last. He turned to Yudhishthira, the eldest of the Pandavas, who stood among the survivors. How many, he asked, had fallen? Yudhishthira answered: one billion, six hundred and sixty million, and twenty thousand men had died in the war, and two hundred and forty thousand one hundred and sixty-five had escaped with their lives. Then the king asked where the fallen had gone.

Yudhishthira, who had received the gift of spiritual sight from the sage Lomasa during his years of wandering, could see where each man had gone. Those who had cast off their bodies gladly in fierce battle had reached the worlds of Indra, king of the gods. Those who met death without joy had found the company of heaven's musicians. Those who fell while turning away from the field, or begging for quarter, had reached the world of the hidden ones. The high-souled warriors who scorned to flee, and walked unarmed against armed foes, had won the radiant worlds of Brahma, the creator. And all the rest who died on the field had gone to the far-off northern world of the Uttara-Kurus. To every death, a place.

Then came the work of the living. The king asked about the friendless dead — those with no one to light their pyres — and Yudhishthira gave his order: let no one perish for want of someone to care for them. And so the pyres were built, of sandalwood and aloe and gathered wood, with ghee and oil and perfumes, silken robes, broken chariots, and heaps of weapons for fuel; and the fires were lit.

Duryodhana and his hundred brothers were burned with the rites due to the dead: Shalya, Jayadratha, Abhimanyu — Arjuna's boy — Duhshasana's son, Bhurishrava, Drupada, Virata, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, and the thousands of the Srinjayas. The smoke of the pyres rose over Kurukshetra, and the field of the great war became, at last, a place of burning and of farewell.
reflection: Krishna's rebuke comes to a woman who has just cursed him, and it refuses to let her grief become a weapon that rewrites what happened. 'A princess bears sons for being slaughtered' is brutal — and it is also the one sentence that could make a queen of the dead stop and hear that her sorrow, however vast, is not the whole story.
next_story_tease: On the road back to Hastinapura, Arjuna would ask Krishna to speak again the teaching he had heard before the war began.
hero_scene: On the field of Kurukshetra, Krishna stands before Gandhari — a queen in mourning, her eyes red with weeping — and speaks to her with open hands and unflinching truth, while the smoke of the first funeral pyres rises behind them into a grey sky.
